summary: This document defines the Subject Identification Method for putting a privacy-sensitive identifier in the subjectAltName extension of an X.509 certificate. Relying parties can optionally use it to check whether a certificate's subject corresponds to a particular sensitive identifier.

plainLanguage.summary: A certificate is like an ID card. This lets the card carry a hidden code, so someone who already knows your secret number can check it is you without it being printed openly.

questions: what is the subject identification method
how to hide a sensitive identifier in a certificate
what is the sim in subjectaltname
subtitle: A way to put a hashed, password-protected personal identifier in a certificate so only the owner can reveal it.

tldr.problem: Relying parties sometimes need to know whether a certificate's subject is the person tied to a sensitive identifier such as a Social Security Number, but that identifier cannot sit in a certificate in plaintext.
tldr.mechanism: A Registration Authority hashes the user's password, a random value, an identifier type and the identifier twice, and the result (the SIM) goes into the subjectAltName extension as an otherName.
tldr.outcome: The subject decides when to reveal the identifier, and a relying party that is given the right inputs can recompute the hash and compare it to the certificate.

facts.label: Formula
facts.value: SIM = R || PEPSI, PEPSI = H(H(P || R || SIItype || SII))

facts.label: Random value R
facts.value: Same length as the hash output (160 bits for SHA-1)

facts.label: Password length
facts.value: Up to 28 characters MUST be allowed

today: RFC 4683 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2006, and no RFC in the unit metadata obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Problem with Names and Sensitive Identifiers
sections.content:
A Certification Authority (CA) binds a public key to a subject through names in the subject or subjectAltName fields of an X.509 certificate. Names are ambiguous: different people and companies can have the same or similar names, so a relying party may find it hard to tie a certificate to one specific person.

An identifier such as a Social Security Number would settle the question, but it is private data and should not appear in a certificate in plaintext. The RFC also notes it is not a true secret, since people disclose such identifiers for certain transactions, for example to open a bank account.

The Subject Identification Method (SIM) and the Privacy-Enhanced Protected Subject Information (PEPSI) format let a certificate carry a protected form of the identifier. The subject controls exposure, and when the subject chooses to reveal it, relying parties can verify the binding.
sections.plainLanguage: Lots of people share the same name, like two kids called Sam in one school. A private ID number would tell them apart, but you do not want to write it where everyone can read it.

sections.title: Security and Usability Requirements
sections.content:
The RFC frames the design with a cast: Alice holds a certificate and a sensitive identifier, Bob is a relying party, Eve is an attacker who gets the certificate, and a Registration Authority (RA) and a CA take part in issuance.

  • Alice can prove her identifier to Bob.
  • Eve faces a large work factor to recover it, even if Alice picks a weak password.
  • Nothing Eve learns from one certificate helps her attack another.
  • The CA learns the identifier only when it has to validate what the RA passed on, and treats the SIM as one more name form in subjectAltName.
  • Alice cannot find another identifier and password that assert a false value with her certificate.

On usability, any custom processing happens at the relying party, so Alice can use unmodified commercial software such as a standard browser.
sections.plainLanguage: The goal is a lock that you can open for a friend when you want to, that a stranger cannot pick, and that works even in an ordinary web browser.

sections.title: How the SIM Is Computed
sections.content:
The SIM is defined as R || PEPSI, where PEPSI = H(H(P || R || SIItype || SII)). Here H is a cryptographic hash, P is a password the user chooses, R is a random number from the RA, SIItype is an object identifier saying what kind of identifier it is, and SII is the sensitive identification information itself.

Alice gives P, SIItype and SII to the RA over a secure channel. The RA validates the SIItype and SII, generates R, builds the SIM and sends it to Alice out of band and to the CA. The CA puts it in the certificate.

A new R MUST be generated for each SIM, and its length MUST equal the hash output length (160 bits for SHA-1). Implementations MUST let users choose passwords of up to 28 characters. Both SHA-1 and SHA-256 MUST be supported, and SHA-1 or SHA-256 SHOULD be used where interoperability matters. Before hashing, the password is prepared with a stringprep-based algorithm, with the changes the RFC lists.
sections.plainLanguage: Mix your secret number, your password and a random number together in a blender, and run it twice. Only someone who knows the recipe can rebuild the same smoothie to check it matches.

sections.title: SIM, PEPSI and Encrypted PEPSI Syntax
sections.content:
The SIM is an ASN.1 SEQUENCE of three fields: hashAlg (an algorithm identifier), authorityRandom (the RA-chosen random value) and pEPSI (the hash). It is carried as an otherName in the subject alternative name, with the object identifier id-on-SIM, defined as { id-on 6 }.

The hashed input is an ASN.1 structure called HashContent with userPassword, authorityRandom, identifierType and identifier.

When the CA itself must check the identifier, the RA and the user each send an Encrypted PEPSI (EPEPSI), computed as E(SIItype || SII || SIM). The CA decrypts both and compares them. The RFC does not define the encryption method. In a certificate request the EPEPSI travels in regInfo, identified by id-regEPEPSI.
sections.plainLanguage: The code on the card is written in a fixed form with labelled boxes: which scrambler was used, the random number, and the scrambled result.

sections.title: Three Ways to Use a SIM
sections.content:
The RFC describes three use cases, depending on what the relying party already knows.

  • Bob knows nothing: Alice sends the certificate, P, SIItype and SII over a secure channel. Bob takes R from the SIM, recomputes the hash and compares. Bob learns the identifier.
  • Bob already knows the identifier: Alice sends only the certificate and P, and Bob supplies the SII from his own knowledge.
  • Alice does not want to disclose it: Alice sends the intermediate value H(P || R || SIItype || SII) over a secure channel. Bob applies the hash once more and compares it to the SIM, learning that Alice knows the right identifier and password without learning the identifier.

This check is NOT to be used instead of standard certificate validation, only in addition to it. A certificate request can carry the SIM too, placed in the subjectAltName extension when PKCS#10 is used.
sections.plainLanguage: You can show a friend the whole secret, show them a hint they can check against what they already know, or just prove you know it without saying it out loud.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Confidentiality rests on iterated hashing of R, P and the identifier. The RFC says the then-current attacks by Wang and others on SHA-1 do not apply here, because the user does not supply all the hashed data: the RA provides R.

Many identifiers are short, and an attacker with partial information such as gender, age and date of birth might guess one, while SIItype values are very limited. So the password carries the weight, and users need a fairly good one.

The scheme assumes Bob is trustworthy and will not reuse Alice's information, otherwise he could impersonate her if only knowledge of P and the identifier were checked. It MUST be used only with protocols that use digital signatures made with the subject's private key. When a certificate is renewed, a new R SHOULD be generated, because repeating the SIM lets an attacker link certificates of the same person. Name constraints cannot be applied to this name form.
sections.plainLanguage: A weak password is like a lock anyone can guess, so pick a strong one. Also only show your secret to people you trust, and change the scramble each time you get a new card.
